chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Asam, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Durays had under his authority the daughter of Humran, so he stipulated for her that he would never marry another woman during her lifetime and after her death, on the condition that she stipulated for him that she would not marry after him. So he made upon them both from the Hajj, the offering, the vows, and all wealth they possessed to be given to the poor, and every slave they owned to be freed, if each one of them did not fulfill his obligation to the other. Then he came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and mentioned that to him. He said:

Indeed, for her father Humran is a right, and that will not prevent us from saying the truth. Go, marry and be content, for that is nothing, and there is no burden on you and no burden on her, and that which you did is not binding. So he was content and had children after that.

key_terms.الحَجِّ: Hajj (pilgrimage, often used as a form of expiation or gift)
key_terms.يَتَزَوَّجَ عَلَيْهَا: To marry upon her (remain married to her)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling on a husband's stipulation to remain unmarried to his wife in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a stipulation preventing a husband from taking another wife (polygyny) is not legally binding in a way that restricts his right to remarry, as the condition does not create a permanent prohibition. The Imam dismisses the substantial financial penalties (such as freeing slaves or giving wealth) attached to the breach, emphasizing that the father's right or the specific wording does not override the fundamental permissibility of polygyny and remarriage in Shia jurisprudence. This highlights the principle that marital conditions are often viewed as recommendations or contractual terms rather than absolute legal bars to the husband's statutory rights.
